lessons.title: When can another thread see initialized state?
lessons.explanation: A happens-before relationship guarantees visibility and ordering of the relevant actions across threads. Task submission through an Executor creates such a boundary for actions performed before submission. Future.get also establishes a boundary for the completed computation. These guarantees do not automatically cover changes made by the submitting thread after handing off the task.
lessons.example: A caller fills a payload with value 7, submits a task that reads it, and leaves the payload alone. The task can rely on seeing that initialization. If the caller instead mutates the same value to 9 immediately after submission, the earlier handoff alone does not order the mutation against the read.
lessons.exercise: How would you guarantee the worker always processes the value at submission time?
lessons.answer: Copy the needed value into an immutable task input before submission and avoid sharing mutable nested state. Waiting for the result can establish visibility back to the caller, but does not retroactively freeze an object passed to the task.

lessons.title: Why is a thread pool full while CPU use stays low?
lessons.explanation: A pool has workers that execute tasks and a queue for tasks waiting to start. A worker waiting for another resource still occupies its slot. In ThreadPoolExecutor, an unbounded work queue can make the maximum pool size ineffective after the core workers are active. Queue policy is part of the service's latency contract.
lessons.example: Four fixed workers wait for database connections. Twelve tasks are queued. CPU use can be low while no queued task starts. Capture thread stacks during the wait and compare connection checkout counts, queue depth and oldest task age. Increasing workers could merely move more waiting tasks to the connection pool.
lessons.exercise: With four active workers and a bounded queue of eight already full, a new task arrives. Which caller-visible result should you expect?
lessons.answer: Read the configured rejection policy. AbortPolicy throws RejectedExecutionException, while CallerRunsPolicy may execute the task on the submitting thread when the executor is running. Account for how either behavior changes response time, and test overload after the dependency recovers.

lessons.title: Why does one request see the previous request's context?
lessons.explanation: A ThreadLocal associates a value with the current thread. A pool reuses worker threads across requests. The lifetime of the worker can exceed the lifetime of the user or trace identifier stored on it. A missing cleanup on an exceptional exit can leave stale state for subsequent work.
lessons.example: Worker A handles request 41 and sets its trace label to blue. Its handler throws before cleanup. Request 42 later runs on the same worker and reads the label before setting its own. Its logs can incorrectly say blue. Put the installation and removal around the entire unit of work with a finally block. If code supports nested scopes, restore the previous context on exit.
lessons.exercise: Would a ThreadLocal automatically follow a request that resumes on another worker?
lessons.answer: Ordinary ThreadLocal storage is per thread. Pass the request context explicitly or use a framework propagation mechanism with a defined lifetime. Test both an exceptional exit and a handoff between two named workers.

title: Loading code and diagnosing runtime limits

lessons.title: When are two classes with the same name different types?
lessons.explanation: A class file describes a type by binary name. In a running JVM, class identity also includes its defining class loader. Loading obtains a class definition, linking checks it and prepares it for use, and initialization executes the required class initialization code. An operation that loads a class does not necessarily initialize it.
lessons.example: A host application and a plugin each define their own copy of api.Event. The plugin can print the same class name the host expects and still fail the host cast. Log the defining loader of the interface expected by the host and the defining loader of the interface implemented by the plugin.
lessons.exercise: Both plugins have their own private implementation classes. How can the host accept both through a common interface?
lessons.answer: Arrange for both to resolve the shared API through the same defining loader, while retaining private implementations in the plugin loaders. Prove assignability across the actual plugin boundary. Identical source code or class-file checksums alone do not establish runtime identity.
lessons.sourceTitle: Java Virtual Machine Specification · Loading, linking and initialization

lessons.title: What can a rising heap graph prove?
lessons.explanation: G1 manages the Java heap as regions and collects selected regions, evacuating live objects when appropriate. Allocating rapidly and retaining a growing set of objects cause different problems. Compare comparable workload phases, collection events and the post-collection live-data trend before diagnosing a leak.
lessons.example: During three similar ten-minute intervals, use grows to 700 MiB and falls to 210, 212 and 211 MiB after comparable collections. The peaks alone are weak evidence of unbounded retention. If comparable low points instead rise from 210 to 340 to 475 MiB, inspect reference paths, cache policy and the workload that produced the objects.
lessons.exercise: The JVM process grows while the measured Java heap remains roughly flat. Would raising the heap limit be your first experiment?
lessons.answer: Measure other contributors such as direct buffers, thread stacks and native allocations. Record process memory, heap and collection logs together. Increasing the maximum heap without evidence can leave less headroom for other memory within the container.

lessons.title: Which bottleneck do virtual threads remove?
lessons.explanation: Virtual threads allow a large number of tasks to wait without requiring one permanently occupied platform thread per task. A database connection, CPU core and remote-service quota remain finite resources. Give each constrained dependency an explicit admission policy.
lessons.example: Five hundred concurrent requests use virtual threads, but only ten database connections exist. If each checkout occupies a connection for 50 ms, the idealized ceiling of that pool is about 200 operations per second. This estimate assumes continuous use, one checkout per operation and no other limit. Adding virtual threads cannot multiply the ten connections.
lessons.exercise: How would you test whether the connection pool or the CPU sets the observed limit?
lessons.answer: Sweep concurrency while recording throughput, checkout wait, connection hold time, CPU use and tail latency. Change one resource limit per run. A rising checkout wait with ten busy connections is direct evidence to investigate database demand before increasing concurrency.
